prompt: Which of these should page somebody at night?
hint: Which one does a customer feel?

choices.text: The 95th percentile of booking above 500 ms
choices.why: Right. It is a symptom: people waiting longer than the requirement allows.

choices.text: CPU above 90% on the database host
choices.why: A cause. A busy processor serving every booking in time is not a problem for anybody.

choices.text: A disk three quarters full
choices.why: A cause, and one that grows slowly: a ticket for working hours.

choices.text: One of three servers restarted and came back
choices.why: If the other two served everybody, nobody felt it.

prompt: Lesson 23's slow payment provider left every machine idle. What does that say about alerts on causes?
hint: Which outage did nobody write a cause for?

choices.text: They would have fired, a few minutes late
choices.why: No CPU, memory or disk threshold was crossed, so none would have fired at all.

choices.text: Nobody had written a cause alert for this outage
choices.why: Right. A symptom alert on duration catches it whatever the cause turns out to be.

choices.text: Causes should be alerted on the network rather than on the hosts
choices.why: The network was fine too; the provider was slow.

choices.text: Idle machines are themselves the alert to write
choices.why: Idle machines are normal at night; that alert would fire every evening.

prompt: The SLO is 99.5% of bookings succeeding over 30 days. The error ratio is 2%. What is the burn rate, how many times faster than allowed the budget is being spent?
hint: Divide the ratio by the budget.

prompt: What does for: 2m change about a rule?

choices.text: It evaluates the rule every two minutes
choices.why: Evaluation follows evaluation_interval; for is about how long the condition holds.

choices.text: It sends the alert again every two minutes
choices.why: Repeating is Alertmanager's repeat_interval.

choices.text: It has to hold for two minutes first
choices.why: Right. A blip that falls back within two minutes never pages anybody.

choices.text: It widens the rate() window to two minutes
choices.why: The window is the [5m] inside expr; for does not touch it.

prompt: An alert fires every week and every time the service turns out to be fine. What is the right response?
hint: What does a page that needs no action teach the person?

choices.text: Keep it, since a false alarm is better than a missed one
choices.why: Each false alarm teaches the team to ignore the next real one.

choices.text: Lengthen repeat_interval so it arrives less often
choices.why: It still pages for nothing, only less often.

choices.text: Route it to a second person as well
choices.why: Now two people learn to ignore it.

choices.text: Move the threshold, or delete the alert
choices.why: Right. A page must need a human now; deleting an alert is part of the work.

prompt: Match each part of an alerting rule to what it decides.
hint: The list under the rule file.

pairs.right: how long it must hold before firing
what the person on call reads

right_distractors: how often Prometheus scrapes the target

prompt: promtool check rules says SUCCESS. What has that not shown?
hint: It reads the file; it feeds it nothing.

choices.text: That the rule fires at the moments it is meant to
choices.why: Right. Only a test with series and expected alerts shows that.

choices.text: That the YAML parses
choices.why: That is exactly what it checks.

choices.text: That the PromQL in each expression is valid
choices.why: It parses every expression, so a syntax error fails it.

choices.text: How many rules the file contains
choices.why: It prints that: 2 rules found.

prompt: An alert whose expression is true but whose for: has not yet run out is in the state Prometheus calls ___.
Errors start at minute 10 of the test and the 5-minute ratio passes 2% at minute 12. With for: 5m, when does the alert fire?
hint: for counts from when the expression became true.

choices.text: At minute 15, five minutes after the first error
choices.why: for counts from the expression being true, at 12, not from the first error.

choices.text: At minute 17
choices.why: Right: 12 plus 5. The whole of lesson 1's five minutes, spent before anything is sent.

choices.text: At minute 14, the same as with for: 2m
choices.why: The failing test showed nothing firing at 14.

choices.text: Never, since the ratio falls back first
choices.why: The failures keep growing at 5 a minute; the ratio stays above 2%.

prompt: One payment in three failed, and the alert said about 3%. Why so low?
hint: Which requests are in the bottom of the ratio?

choices.text: Prometheus only samples one request in ten
choices.why: Counters count every request; nothing is sampled.

choices.text: humanizePercentage divides the value by ten
choices.why: It only formats 0.0333 as 3.331%.

choices.text: Bookings were 13.5% of all requests
choices.why: Right, and 409s never reach the payment. A broken journey hides in a healthy average.

choices.text: flaky.py's failures are counted as 409s
choices.why: They are 500s; the log shows status 500 with the exception.

prompt: The alert reached firing, and nobody's phone rang. Why?
hint: Who did Prometheus try to tell?

choices.text: The rule had no runbook_url
choices.why: It had one, and an annotation never stops delivery anyway.

choices.text: for: 2m had not run out yet
choices.why: Firing means it had; pending is the state before.

choices.text: severity: page is not a label Prometheus knows
choices.why: No label needs to be known; routing on it is Alertmanager's job.

choices.text: Nothing was listening on port 9093
choices.why: Right. Prometheus decides that an alert fires; Alertmanager decides who hears, and there was none.

prompt: Match each Alertmanager setting to what it does.
hint: The four jobs under the configuration.

pairs.right: sends page alerts to the person on call
waits for the rest of a group before the first notice
re-sends a firing alert after four hours
holds one alert back while another fires

right_distractors: decides when the rule's expression is true

prompt: What is a dead man's switch for?

choices.text: Paging when a constant alert stops arriving at all
choices.why: Right. Silence is the symptom of a broken alerting path, so silence is what it alerts on.

choices.text: Stopping boxoffice when the error ratio passes 2%
choices.why: Nothing here stops the service; alerts tell people.

choices.text: Muting every alert while somebody deploys
choices.why: That is a silence, and a dangerous habit, not a dead man's switch.

choices.text: Escalating to a manager after ten minutes
choices.why: That is an escalation policy, in the paging service.

prompt: Put a runbook's four questions in the order it answers them.
hint: From what it means to whom to call.
items: who to call when that fails

prompt: Why is a postmortem written without blame?
hint: What happens to the next mistake if this one is punished?

choices.text: Because nobody is ever at fault in an incident
choices.why: People make mistakes; the question is why the system let a reasonable one through.

choices.text: So mistakes are told, and the system changes
choices.why: Right. Blame teaches people to hide the next mistake, and a hidden one cannot be learnt from.

choices.text: Because the law forbids naming the people involved
choices.why: No law is the reason; it is a working rule.

choices.text: So the incident can be closed faster
choices.why: Speed is not the point; learning is.

prompt: The primary on call does not acknowledge a page within ten minutes. In an escalation policy, what happens?

choices.text: The page is dropped until the next evaluation
choices.why: Dropping a page is how an outage goes unnoticed.

choices.text: Prometheus lowers the threshold
choices.why: Thresholds are in the rule file; nothing changes them at runtime.

choices.text: The paging service calls the secondary
choices.why: Right, and after the secondary, a manager.

choices.text: Alertmanager inhibits the alert
choices.why: Inhibition is about another alert firing, not about nobody answering.

prompt: The provider starts failing one call in ten. The overall ratio sits near 1% and nothing fires, while a tenth of payers are turned away. What is the best change?

choices.text: Lower the overall threshold from 2% down to 0.5% for the service
choices.why: It would page on noise from every route, and still hide a smaller failure of bookings.

choices.text: Raise for: to ten minutes so that the alert is quite sure
choices.why: The ratio never crosses 2%; waiting longer changes nothing.

choices.text: Alert on the payment provider's CPU
choices.why: A cause, on a machine you do not own.

choices.text: A second rule on the booking route's own error ratio
choices.why: Right. The journey that earns the money gets its own symptom and threshold.

prompt: Which of these are spent inside lesson 1's five minutes? Choose every one that is.
hint: The figure of the time budget.

choices.text: the two minutes of for
choices.why: Yes, the largest block.

choices.text: Alertmanager's group_wait
choices.why: Yes, 30 seconds.

choices.text: the repeat_interval of four hours
choices.why: No: it applies after the first notice, to repeats.

choices.text: scraping the failures and evaluating the rule
choices.why: Yes, a few seconds each.

choices.text: writing the postmortem
choices.why: No: that comes after the incident.

prompt: What did all four thirds of this course do before running their tools?

choices.text: Turned an adjective into a number or a named list
choices.why: Right: a percentile, WCAG 2.2 AA, the OWASP risks, an error ratio with a time to reach a person.

choices.text: Installed every tool from Ubuntu's archive
choices.why: Several came from elsewhere; installing was never the hard part.

choices.text: Ran the tool once first, to see what kind of result it gave
choices.why: That is writing the requirement around the number you got, which lesson 1 warned against.

choices.text: Agreed that a person reviews each result
choices.why: People read some results, but the move was to make a machine able to say fail.
